title: Milk and blood
hookLine: tradition says he squeezed Lalo's bread and milk ran out, and from Bhago's feast, blood

cards: A tense room in Saidpur. Malik Bhago, the rich official, has summoned Guru Nanak to explain himself: why eat a carpenter's coarse bread and snub my feast? The townspeople crowd in.
Everyone wants to see what happens when a holy man with nothing insults a man with everything. And here, as tradition tells it, the dinner-party drama becomes something stranger.
Nanak asks for two things: a piece of Lalo's bread, and a piece of food from Bhago's table. He takes one in each hand.

teach.b: Tradition says he pressed them. From Lalo's bread, milk ran out. From Bhago's rich food, blood.
That's the whole scene, told in gurdwaras and children's books and painted on walls. Sikhs read it in more than one way. Some take it as a miracle that really happened, a sign given to a proud man.

Others read it as a picture, a parable in the language of the janamsakhis, which are full of wonders. Plainly put, the milk and the blood aren't in the scripture itself; they come from the later life stories.

What the scripture has is the idea underneath, in Guru Nanak's own words. In one hymn, he says that taking what rightfully belongs to another is as forbidden as pork is to a Muslim and beef is to a Hindu.
He reaches for the one thing each of his neighbors would never eat, and says: that's what stolen wealth is. So in either reading, the point is the same. Food carries its history.
Lalo's bread came from sweat, and it nourishes, like milk.
Bhago's feast came from taxes and bribes and squeezing people who had little, so in the story's startling picture, it's made of their blood.

teach.h: MIRACLE OR PARABLE: SIKHS READ BOTH.
teach.b: Nobody could see it on the plate.
The story makes it visible, and asks a question that doesn't expire: not how much, or how nice, but how was it earned?
Tradition says Bhago was shaken, and changed his ways.

how: Sikhs tell the milk-and-blood sakhi as a teaching about honest earnings; many gurdwaras and families use it to explain why kirat, honest work, matters, and some Sikhs give a tenth of their income, dasvandh, from earnings made honestly.

o: what rightfully belongs to someone else
a tax that officials collected from farmers
a blessing given with food at the gurdwara

games.q: what came from each hand — tap the pairs.
p: like pork or beef to the faithful
where the milk and blood are told

s: the milk and blood appear in the Guru Granth Sahib
they come from the later life stories. the scripture has the idea underneath, not the scene.
Sikhs all read the story the same way
some take it as a real miracle; others read it as a parable. the point is the same.
Nanak compared stolen wealth to forbidden food
taking another's rightful due is like pork to a Muslim, beef to a Hindu.

games.q: you're Malik Bhago. the Guru has just pressed your fine food and blood has run out of it, in front of the whole town. what do you do?
o: laugh it off as a trick.
take it to heart and change your ways.
games.why: tradition says Bhago was shaken and changed. the story isn't about ruining him; it's about letting him see.

practice: Pick one thing near you, your shoes, your phone, the chair, and trace it back as far as you can: who made it, where, who carried it, who was paid, and who maybe wasn't. You won't know all of it, and that's fine.
Follow it as far as it goes, without guilt and without a verdict.

wordCard.voice: Hakk. What rightfully belongs to another, the idea behind the milk and blood tradition says ran from Lalo's honest bread and Bhago's stolen feast.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: hakk, what rightfully belongs to someone, from Arabic haqq; the word in Nanak's line about another's due.

carryVoice: Your line: how was it earned. Tomorrow, a rest house on the road. That's thirty-four days.

sources.ref: Janamsakhi traditions (milk from Lalo's bread, blood from Bhago's food)
Guru Granth Sahib, Var Majh, salok of Guru Nanak, Ang 141 (another's due like pork and beef)
